issues.legal_issue: A court sale certificate that clearly identifies property by boundaries transfers the entire property within those boundaries, and a general description of the property does not confine the sale to only one structure within them.
material_facts: The property was sold in execution of a money decree, and the sale certificate described it by clear boundaries as well as by a property name, number, and the words “terraced house.”
The judgment debtor argued that only the terraced building had been sold and that a separate building and vacant site within the stated boundaries had not been included.
The executing court found, after examining the sale certificate and other documents, that the entire property within the boundaries had been sold.
issues.conclusion: The sale certificate covered the entire property within its stated boundaries; it could not be confined to only the structure described as the terraced house.
issues.legal_principle: A sale certificate is a document of title that should not be lightly regarded or loosely construed (Rambhadra Naidu v. Kadiriyasami Naicker, (1921) LR 48 IA 155). Where boundaries and another identifying description are both given, a discrepancy or generality in the latter does not alter the identity of the property conveyed when the boundaries clearly identify it (Sheodhyan Singh v. Musammat Sanichara Kuer, 1962 (2) SCR 753). The description “terraced house” was not precise enough to exclude other structures and land lying within the stated boundaries.

predicates.execution_sale_certificate_dispute: A party disputed in an execution proceeding what property a court-issued sale certificate conveyed.
predicates.sale_certificate_has_clear_boundaries: The sale certificate stated boundaries that clearly identified the property sold.
predicates.certificate_uses_general_structure_descr: The sale certificate also used a general description of a structure that did not precisely define the property's extent.
predicates.objector_claims_only_one_structure_was_s: A party claimed that only one structure within the stated boundaries had been sold, excluding other property within them.

issues.definition: When an execution-sale dispute involves clear certificate boundaries, a general structure description, and a claim that only one structure was sold, the sale covers the entire property within the boundaries.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court cannot reopen the executing court’s factual finding about what property was sold when that finding was reached by examining the sale certificate and other documents.
material_facts: The executing court examined the sale certificate and other documents and found that the entire property within the stated boundaries had been sold.
The High Court, in revision, set aside that determination and remitted the matter for a local inspection to establish whether another building and vacant site existed within the boundaries.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reopening the executing court’s finding of fact; its orders were set aside and the executing court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: What was sold in execution of a decree is a question of fact (S.M. Jakati v. S.M. Borkar, 1959 SCR 138). The High Court, exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, was not justified in reopening the executing court’s factual finding in this case.

predicates.execution_proceeding_revision: A party sought revision of an executing court's order concerning the scope of a court sale.
predicates.executing_court_made_factual_sale_scope_: The executing court determined as a fact what property had been sold.
predicates.finding_based_on_sale_documents: The executing court based its determination on examining the sale certificate and other relevant documents.

issues.definition: When revision concerns an execution proceeding and the executing court determined the scope of the sale from the relevant documents, the revisional court cannot reopen that factual determination.
